narrative:
The model predicted a 72% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest influence. Standing in the bottom decile for both years—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. This academic performance signal outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30, which is actually slightly above the average of accepted students, worked in your favor and pulled the prediction somewhat toward passing. Similarly, coming from an upper-middle income family, which is the most common background among accepted applicants, also nudged the outcome mildly in a positive direction. However, these encouraging factors were not nearly enough to overcome the substantial negative impact of your class standing.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Retaking key courses, enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program, or gaining substantial work experience that demonstrates analytical ability could improve your profile for future applications. Consider reaching out to the admissions office to discuss specific steps that have helped similar candidates succeed.
